title: Mass intentions
hookLine: a Mass can be offered for someone living or dead; any offering is a gift, not a price

lines: THE BACK PAGE OF THE BULLETIN.
THIS MASS IS OFFERED FOR MARIA.
cards: The back page of a parish bulletin, under the Mass times. Saturday evening: for Maria Lopez, deceased. Sunday morning: for the Kowalski family.

Tuesday: in thanksgiving, for a safe surgery. Wednesday: for a grandmother, on her birthday. On Saturday evening the priest says it aloud, near the start or in the prayers: this Mass is offered for Maria.
A few people in the pews look up. One of them is the one who asked. What does it mean to say a Mass is for someone?
And what about the envelope that went to the parish office?

teach.b: Start with an old root. In the second book of Maccabees, after a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection and sends the silver to Jerusalem so a sacrifice can be offered for the soldiers who died.

That's the passage that closed with yesterday's holy and wholesome thought. Catholics see in it the shape of a Mass intention: an offering, a sacrifice, and a particular person held up to God. Who can a Mass be for?
Anyone: a sick friend, a newborn, a marriage on its anniversary, a soldier far away.
Church law says a priest is free to apply the Mass for anyone, living or dead. It doesn't have to be a Catholic. Then the envelope.
Church law allows a priest to accept an offering from someone who asks for a Mass for their intention, but insists there must be no hint of trade or commerce in it.
The offering is a gift that supports the Church and its priests, not a price that buys a Mass.

The law even urges priests to celebrate Mass for the intentions of the faithful, especially the poor, without receiving any offering at all. If you can't give, you can still ask. Last, what an intention does.
Saturday's Mass isn't a different Mass, and Maria isn't the only person it touches.
The whole Church prays, and Christ's offering is the same.
The intention names one face inside it, like holding up one photograph in a crowded room and saying, especially her.

how: Catholics ask a parish to have a Mass offered for a living or deceased person, usually through the parish office, and the intention is often listed in the bulletin or mentioned at that Mass. Some give an offering when they ask; Church law forbids any appearance of buying the Mass and urges priests to accept intentions from the poor without one.

o: a private Mass held for one paying family
the reason a priest gives for his homily
a Mass offered for one person, living or dead

p: sent silver for a sacrifice for the dead
one person named inside the Mass
priests are urged to offer Mass for them

s: a Mass can only be offered for a Catholic
Church law says a priest is free to apply the Mass for anyone, living or dead.
the offering pays for the Mass
Church law excludes any appearance of trade; the offering is a gift that supports the Church.
a priest may celebrate Mass for someone's intention with no offering at all
the law urges priests to do this, especially for the poor.

games.q: you want a Mass offered for your father, who just died, but you have no money to spare this month. what does Church law say?
o: you'll have to wait until you can pay.
priests are urged to celebrate Mass for the intentions of the faithful, especially the poor, without an offering.
games.why: the law urges exactly that, and forbids any hint of trade in offerings. you can still ask.

practice: Ask who comes to mind first: someone who has died, someone sick, someone starting something new, someone you worry about and can't help. Let one person settle, hold their face, and wish them every good thing for one long breath.
If you're Catholic, or would like to be part of this, you might plan to call a parish office and ask for a Mass for them; if not, keep them close.

wordCard.voice: Mass intentions. Asking a priest to offer a Mass for a particular person, living or dead, often with an offering given as a gift, never as a price. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the application of the Mass: the Church's term for offering a Mass for a particular intention.

carryVoice: Your line: a mass for them. One face, named inside the whole Church's prayer. Back tomorrow, same hill.
